title: Single global clock domain with no feedback, tuned trees driving one grid
where_in_paper: Clock design and Global clock distribution network
decision: Use single chip-wide global clock domain with no skew feedback or adjustment settings, consisting of buffered H-trees from central PLL to 64 carefully placed sector buffers, each driving tunable sector tree network of ~2000 tunable transmission lines, all driving a single full-chip clock grid at 1024 evenly spaced points to 15200 global clock pins
alternatives_or_rejected: Multiple clock domains with feedback-adjustable deskew or phase alignment, or symmetric H-tree only; paper says strategy was extension of previous server designs achieving unexcelled measured jitter and skew without adjustment circuitry
rationale: Simple clock timing and rapid bringup facilitated by neglecting modeled skew and using constant clock uncertainty across whole chip; tuning via patented algorithm on transmission line widths; top-down grid contract early insulates designers from later grid changes, while bottom-up macro/unit/chip routing can still respond to late changes
outcome: Measured 20ps skew (20-40ps long distance), 35ps total jitter from PLL plus distribution, <10ps cycle compression from PLL alone, ability to use constant uncertainty and correct-by-design methodology; 150ps chip-to-chip jitter

title: SOI-specific PLL placed at center with on-chip analog supply
where_in_paper: Clock design - PLL and global clock distribution
decision: Place single SOI-optimized PLL near center of chip to minimize distribution delay, generate on-chip analog power supply using capacitor mounted on surface of chip module, oscillator runs at twice chip frequency divided by 2 to generate 50% duty cycle global clock
alternatives_or_rejected: Multiple PLLs distributed or bulk-CMOS PLL without SOI adaptations; paper notes previous design adapted, primary focus was adding body contacts to analog circuits while minimizing body resistance and device width uncertainty
rationale: SOI floating-body effects require body contacts in analog; capacitor structures modified with thicker oxide and recessed-oxide opening layout to maintain leakage acceptable; center placement minimizes global delay and enables symmetric H-trees
outcome: SOI PLL design resulted in less than 10ps compression from PLL and 35ps total compression, 20ps skew, verified via top-metal probe pads and direct probing of 100 probe pads and global buffer outputs

title: Primarily static circuit design style, dynamic only sparingly
decision: Adopt primarily static circuit design strategy, with dynamic circuits used only sparingly in SRAMs and other critical regions of processor core, despite aggressive 1.3+ GHz target in 0.18um CMOS 8S3 SOI
alternatives_or_rejected: Highly dynamic design as used in prior high-frequency microprocessors; paper discusses that size/complexity (174M transistors) and SOI floating-body effect and noise immunity concerns pushed away from dynamic
rationale: Sheer size, complexity and transistor count placed constraints; uncertainties associated with modeling floating-body effect and its impact on noise immunity and overall chip decoupling capacitance requirements favored static; static also eases timing methodology and multisite verification
outcome: Met cycle time target with custom design for most dataflow macros and logic synthesis for control, enabled transistor-level timing and noise analysis methodology, met schedule with hierarchical design

title: Four-level hierarchical methodology with contracts for multisite design
where_in_paper: Design methodology and Design flow and tools
decision: Organize physical and logical hierarchy into macro (50k transistors typical), unit (~50 macros), core (6 units), chip (2 cores + memory subsystem), with explicit contracts as early size and timing budgets and floorplan abstracts including blockage maps, enabling concurrent design across six IBM sites via Common Tools Environment (CTE)
alternatives_or_rejected: Flat chip design or single-site iteration; paper says complexity 5-10x greater than chips available when design started straining capabilities of design team, methodology, tools
rationale: Allows logic design/simulation to progress in parallel with circuit design at each level, floorplanning and timing to begin in parallel with higher-level logic; contracts allow refined floorplannable objects, R and C estimates for wires, enabling concrete physical design with engineered buses; 1015 unique macros / 4341 total, 442 custom, 523 RLM random-logic macros built via BooleDozer + Cadence physically aware synthesis
outcome: Consistent contracts across hierarchy by end of high-level design, complete transistor-level schematics for macros with near-final sizing, daily iterated timing flow during physical design phase, successful 174M transistor 1.3GHz chip in 0.18um 7-layer copper

title: Transistor-level timing and verification with macro audit grading
where_in_paper: Design methodology - verification and Figure 3-5 flows
decision: Time all custom macros at transistor level using Pathmill, electrical rule checking via EinsCheck tool, noise via Harmony, formal verification via Verity (transistor netlist vs VHDL) and test model via GateMaker, physical verification via Niagara (DRC/LVS/methodology/yield), plus SKILL methodology checks, with elaborate audit system grading each macro A/B/C/D/F on 26 tools requiring A before release (16000 grades)
alternatives_or_rejected: Block-based timing with pessimistic guardband or gate-level timing only; paper notes by timing at transistor level inaccuracies and needless pessimism avoided, which is especially challenging for large high-frequency chip with long wires requiring several cycles to traverse
rationale: High-frequency goal placed stringent requirements on circuits and long wires in noisy environment; each macro run serves two purposes: detailed report of timing/noise and generation of timing/noise rules for upper levels; need to synchronize design environment across multisite team and ensure production readiness of >1000 macros
outcome: Meaningful first-pass standard-cell macro timings, final parasitic-extraction-based timing rules, detailed abstracts with macro sizes and complete metal blockage maps; 500 of macros synthesized RLMs, remaining custom; enabled final unit/chip wiring and extraction and complete verification against simulated logic
